title: Unweighted Gapped Clique Homology is $\mathsf{QMA}_1$-complete
abstract: Deciding whether the clique complex of a given graph has nontrivial homology in a given dimension, under vertex-product weighting and an inverse-polynomial spectral gap promise on the combinatorial Hodge Laplacian, is known to be $\mathsf{QMA}_1$-hard and contained in $\mathsf{QMA}$ by King and Kohler (FOCS 2024). The vertex weights are essential in the known proof, where they provide the scale separation needed for the spectral gap analysis. We prove that, when every vertex has weight one, the problem remains $\mathsf{QMA}_1^{g_2}$-hard and is contained in $\mathsf{QMA}_1^{g_2}$, where $\mathsf{QMA}_1^{g_2}$ is $\mathsf{QMA}_1$ with the universal gate set $g_2=\{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{CX},\mathsf{CCX},H\otimes H\}$. The construction replaces weight by expansion: each vertex of the weighted complex is blown up into a clique whose size encodes its weight. The block sizes are chosen so that symmetric averages reproduce the weighted Hodge metric. The symmetric sector therefore carries the weighted Laplacian up to a common scalar factor, while a local averaging argument gives a uniform lower bound on the orthogonal complement to the symmetric sector. Hence the weighted gap analysis transfers to an unweighted clique complex without introducing either additional low-energy states or spurious homology. Containment in $\mathsf{QMA}_1^{g_2}$ follows from Rudolph's exact linear combination of unitaries simulation of sparse integer clique Laplacians. The result shows that the gap promise, rather than vertex weighting, is the source of the complexity of gapped clique homology.
summary: The paper proves that deciding the homology of an unweighted clique complex, given a spectral gap promise on its Laplacian, is $\mathsf{QMA}_1$-complete. It achieves this by showing that the complexity originates from the gap condition itself, not from vertex weights, using sophisticated blow-up constructions to map quantum Hamiltonian gaps onto topological invariants.
main_problem: The paper tackles the computational complexity of determining if a graph's clique complex has nontrivial homology, especially when spectral gap promises are involved.
main_result: It proves that Unweighted Gapped Clique Homology is $\mathsf{QMA}_1$-complete, demonstrating that the difficulty stems from the spectral gap promise rather than vertex weighting.
method: The proof uses a 'blow-up' construction to transform weighted homology problems into unweighted ones, relying on detailed spectral analysis of the Hodge Laplacian.
model_or_system: The model involves clique complexes derived from graphs ($Cl(G)$) and their associated combinatorial Hodge Laplacians ($\Delta_k$). The complexity is linked to quantum computation via Hamiltonian gap properties.
key_observables: Homology group $H_k(X; \mathbb{R})$ (non-trivial vs. trivial), minimum eigenvalue of the Laplacian $\lambda_{\min}(\Delta_k)$, and spectral gaps ($p(N)$).
important_parameters: Vertex weights, gap size promise ($1/	ext{poly}(N)$), and the universal gate set $g_2$ for $\mathsf{QMA}_1^{g_2}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a source Hamiltonian whose spectral properties can be mapped to the homology gaps via the blow-up construction.
figures_summary: Figure 3 schematically illustrates a single-projector filling gadget, showing how an interior membrane nullifies a boundary cycle while preserving orthogonal cycles.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing hardness for weighted complexes, then developing the 'blow-up' construction to eliminate weights, and finally proving both $\mathsf{QMA}_1$-hardness (via gap preservation) and containment in $\mathsf{QMA}_1^{g_2}$.
why_interesting: This work connects deep concepts from algebraic topology (homology), spectral theory (Laplacians/gaps), and quantum complexity theory ($\mathsf{QMA}$), providing a powerful tool for classifying computational problems arising from physical structures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The blow-up correspondence. A weighted base complex is replaced by an unweighted expanded complex in which vertex weights are represented by block sizes. For simplicity, only the expanded vertices and incomplete edges are drawn. Symmetric averages over one-copy-per- block choices reconstruct the weighted Hodge metric. The illustration uses block sizes 6 and 3, exhibiting an integral ratio of 2.

Figure 2: The qubit-register blow-up. A one-qubit bowtie has two harmonic cycles representing |0⟩and |1⟩. In the expanded register, each vertex is replaced by a complete graph and each bowtie edge by the corresponding complete bipartite connection. The n-qubit register is the join product of these one-qubit expanded graphs. Each register block has size M = ρ; the displayed copy counts are schematic.

Figure 3: A schematic single-projector filling gadget. The boundary cycle is filled by an interior membrane, so the selected encoded cycle becomes null-homologous while the orthogonal cycles are preserved by the selectivity argument. The drawing suppresses the cut-and-reglue triangu- lation and clique-closure data used in that argument.
